title: Help with going beyond html? 3d acceleration with Sol/Opus.
author: crumbaker
selftext:
I've been able to make some amazing things lately I can't wait to share on here, but I want to take things to the next level.   
  
I'm going to be importing some models/textures in a game where html isn't going to cut it. What's the best way to direct these ai's to use 3d acceleration instead of the normal three.js route that creates everything in a simple html file?

Any help from those that have pulled this off is greatly appreciated.

comments.author: ReindeerOk2009
comments.body: As in a model file like .glb? Three.js can handle 3d models if you're going web route. Otherwise regular game engines like Unity/Unreal also handle them. If you're walking about GPU acceleration then some users may need enable hardware acceleration in their browser so that their browser can utilise the GPU

replies.author: crumbaker
replies.body: Not going web route, and I'm trying to get the browser out of the equation so it uses 3d acceleration by default, not cpu rendering like three.js typically uses.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body: Three.js uses GPU, either with WebGPU or WebGL

replies.author: crumbaker
replies.body: so you just tell it specifically to use webgpu or webgl and that's it? Because I told sol to use webgl with three.js at one point and it definitely did not use the gpu when running just cpu rendering.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body: Three.js uses WebGPU with a WebGL fallback. It does not support software rendering. The only way you could get it to do software rendering is if you were running it on a software WebGL or WebGPU implementation (like LLVMpipe).

comments.author: Manjoe70
comments.body: Canvas + webgpu but you really should be looking at using pixi.js or something don’t re-invent the wheel.

replies.author: crumbaker
replies.body: I've never even heard of pixi.js, and I'm a game developer prior to ai lol. So do I just tell the ai to use it?

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
I’m currently working on a 3D game. I would go the three.js route if you’re starting with a game that runs in the browser. 

If you’re making a game that runs outside the browser, I would use Unity or Godot. 

It’s also possible to use 3D APIs directly if you know what you are doing, but in my experience I have had to do a lot more debugging and work, even with AI handling the implementation. The other week I spent two days debugging a blank screen that only showed up on some computers.

replies.author: crumbaker
replies.body: Weird in my experience three.js is not using it, and I am a UE5 dev but I'm trying to create products outside of it.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body: Three.js requires 3D acceleration and does not work without it.

replies.author: tabaxi_gf
replies.body: Are you sure it is not using it or you just think that because it’s slow?
